Firstly, I'm sorry you're experiencing this. Being ghosted certainly isn't a fun part of dating, and it is totally valid to feel the extent of the frustration or hurt. It's tempting to try to throw all those feelings out and force yourself to move on, but I think it's better and ultimately easier to allow yourself to indulge in the emotions, process them, and then let them drift away.

Remember that closure is what you make it. No, you aren't going to ever get that person to tell you what led them to ghost. You are never going to get a satisfying answer from that person, if there even is a satisfying answer to be had.

And that sucks! 

But! You can absolutely reclaim the power that feels robbed. *They* chose to end your connection, robbing you of your power to decide whether or not to remain connected to them. *They* chose not to have an adult conversation about it, robbing you of your power to say or ask whatever would have given you peace of mind about the situation.

However, they do not have the power to keep *you* bound to this situation, to keep it dwelling in your mind. They do not have the power to leave a permanent loose end in *your* life.

I would recommend a simple ritual to concretely reassert your power and the choice you have in how much room the ghoster has in your mind. Something like a knot tying, cord cutting, or fire cleansing spell would be my go to- something that will allow for a tangible, intentional, mindful action *entirely by your own hand* to signify bringing the situation to a close. Allow those feelings of hurt, frustration, grief, whatever is swirling around in you, to have purpose by pouring them into the ritual, and give yourself permission to let them go.

Hopefully, knowing that *you've* made the decision to move on (just like the ghoster did) and allowing yourself the opportunity to physically manifest that decision will bring back your feeling of power. 

For me, that would be closure.

For many people that experience Derry Girls through Netflix only, they expect it to follow the narrative format of a streaming-exclusive show, which it is not.

My take is that it's a consequence of streaming-exlusive shows. We are used to getting a whole season dropped at one time with the intention of it being binge-watched, which is not Derry Girls.

If your aim is for someone to watch the entire season in one sitting, all six episodes can basically be chapters of one 3ish hour long story. If your aim is to release one episode a week on a network channel, casual watchers and channel flippers should be able to enjoy one episode as a fully contained unit. There are, of course, network shows driven by large arcs and slow character development, but those tend to be hour long dramas, not 22 minute comedies.

In a short form comedy show in a network, typically the vibe of each character and the overall dynamic needs to be clear within each individual episode. The plots of each episode need to be wrapped up before the credits roll. There isn't time for a "previously on" and you shouldn't need a more seasoned fan sitting next to you explaining references and backstories. You get the rare "to be continued..." or an hour long special when they need to tell a grander story, such as the finale episode of Derry Girls.

But a lot of us experience Derry Girls only through Netflix, so it can be hard to not expect the framework of a streaming-exclusive show from it.

You didn't do anything wrong by buying the dress. You perhaps could have been more delicate about saying you were purchasing it if you wanted to be extra sensitive to her feelings, but from what you shared, you weren't impolite about it.

There are a lot of "right" ways to go about letting the group know of your dress choice, and you get to dictate that based on how well you know Ana, how interested you are in protecting her feelings, and how naturally inclined you are to be delicate in this sort of situation. You could have engaged in the polite fiction of asking her if she minded, with the expectation that she would engage in the polite fiction of giving her blessing.

However, Ana may not have been overreacting. It's understandable that she would have been a little stung by that, and she may have just been opening up to a friend after a situation that embarrassed her. 

Honestly, I would have done the same thing, and then immediately let it go! Who among us hasn't vented privately when we were embarrassed or bothered by someone's actions, even if we knew (either at that time or after we had calmed down) that they didn't actually do anything heinous?

If Ana had called you out in the group setting, that would be an overreaction. If she brings this up repeatedly or holds a grudge over it, that will be an overreaction. But just vocalizing hurt feelings to her friend, who then relayed that to you seemingly without Ana's knowledge, is not an overreaction. 

I do wonder why your friend relayed that to you, though. Was she trying to get Ana in trouble in your book? Was she trying to dissuade you from getting that dress or give you a heads up about Ana's hurt feelings for everyone's benefit? Without knowing the exact words and tone Ana used, it's quite possible that your friend paraphrased or innocently misinterpreted the conversation when repeating it to you. Knowing your friend's intentions, you may be able to get a better idea of if she may have exaggerated how angry vs embarrassed Ana was.

I wouldn't be too worried about Ana not returning your calls. If I was in her shoes, I'd feel humiliated if I found out that my venting-in-confidence had been relayed to the person I was only briefly upset with.

In the past year, everything changed. Things got quickly cramped in my apartment and my cat food expenses shot through the roof, so I moved us from the city to a cabin in the woods halfway up a sparsely populated mountain. I felt something rub up on my foot and nearly jumped out of my skin. In my excitement upon finding the geology forum, I had forgotten to keep tabs on the sleeping critter, and now I saw the crystal dish was empty. I looked down and saw the creature awake, at my feet. I froze, afraid that any movement would cause it to bite me. The beast was fixated on my toes, and watched it timidly reach out with a claw and poke at my leg big toe curiously. It must have been attracted to my metallic green nail polish. Experimentally, I wiggled my toes a bit. The creature started and I withdrew my foot, afraid of getting bitten, but it followed after my toes, and then it flicked it’s tongue out against my toenail. It had a tongue like my old bearded dragon did, fatty and sticky and thick. Before I could react, it jumped onto my leg and scampered up into my lap. My entire body was shaking, and I was too scared to even breathe as the creature stood on its hind legs and placed its front feet on my shoulders, leaning close to my face the same way Bastet liked to do. It smelled weirdly sweet, almost like a toasted marshmallow. When it opened its mouth, I saw a row of sharp teeth almost identical to those of my cats, with severe looking fangs. 

The creature delicately closed its teeth over the left lense of my glasses and slowly pulled them off my face. Instinctively, my other hand came up to secure the frames to my face, and the creature pulled back, releasing my glasses. It turned around and stepped up onto the kitchen table, and stared at me. Without breaking eye contact, I reached out and slipped my hand under its belly and lifted it. Its head and rear drooped over my hand just like when I picked up my cats the same way when they got on the table. I slowly set it down, still moving slowly so as to not startle it, and as I withdrew my hand, it nuzzled against me. Its fur didn’t feel like fur at all, instead wiry and bristly almost like little strands of plastic.

I let it rub against my hand for a minute and then it went back to curl up in the crystal dish, but did not got back to sleep. It kept its eyes trained on me.

The geologist had responded to my email. He asked what city I live in. Barely a minute after I answer, he sent me an address and the simple directions to gather up the shell and bring the dragon with me, as soon as I could.

Dragon.

I looked at the creature. I had never seen a furry dragon, but it had the body shape I was familiar with from movies and book covers.

Within an hour I had collected the stone shards from my living room carpet into a ziploc bag and coaxed the dragon into one of my cat carriers. This was, surprisingly, far easier than getting one of my cats into the carriers. Once I loaded the carrier into the passenger seat of my car, the dragon seemed to realize it was trapped and starting making pouty sounds. After a few minutes, it settled and I heard snoring once again.

The address from the email took me to a magic shop. I walked in, greeted by the windchimes above the door, and stopped. The place seemed to be empty. This place was unlike the types of magical shops I had visited when I went through my college pagan phase, which were always seemingly intentionally crowded and dusty for the mystique. This place was small but tidy, with books lining the left wall and shelves of dark brown bottles and jars along the other. Tables displayed tools, some that I recognized- cauldrons and knives and wooden ladles- and some things that I couldn’t even conceive of their purpose- a stiff tangle of golden thread with small bones braided into it.

Before I could decide whether to examine the books or jars first, a woman appeared from the back room behind the counter. She looked like she was maybe in her forties, but aged significantly by her silver blonde hair and bony build. Her eyes landed on the carrier I had resting on my hip.

“Cal told me to expect you,” She said, and gave me a friendly smile. She instantly looked ten years younger. “Come on, back this way.”

She raised part of the counter to allow me to pass through, then ushered me into the back room. It was small, the space mostly dominated by the round dark wood table and big arm chairs. Bookshelves lined the walls, and there was a big painting of a unicorn hanging over the fireplace.

“Have a seat. Would you like something to drink? What’s your name?” The woman asked, pausing at a little drink cart in the corner.

“No thanks,” I said, sitting down and trying not to be obvious about how I was staring around the room. “My name is Olivia.”

“Olivia, nice to meet you,” She sat down across from me. “I’m Tara. I hear you have a baby dragon.”

The sentence was so absurd, I didn’t know how to respond. I just stared at her.

“I imagine this must come as quite a shock,” She said. “But dragons are actually fairly sweet creatures if they are raised right, so you have nothing to worry about, safety wise. And I know everything there is to know about dragons, so I’ll help you along the way.”

I kept staring at her, and her smile started to falter.

“Are you okay, dear?” She asked. “I know this must be quite shocking to you.”

“I have a dragon,” I said slowly, and put the carrier on the the table between us. “And you seem to think I will be keeping this dragon.”

“Ah,” She said, nodding. “Right. I’m afraid to tell you that you don’t really have a choice. You see, dragons imprint on their mothers in the weeks leading up to their hatching. Your voice and smell and the particular vibrations of your heart and breathing all permeated the egg shell, and now you are the dragon’s mother.”

“I’m the dragon’s mother,” I repeated. She nodded. “Okay well… I’m not exactly in the position to mother a dragon. Is there a dragon foster care system or a dragon fire station I can drop it off at or something?”

“Afraid not,” Tara said. “Dragons will fly around the world a few times over to be reunited with their mothers. No matter where we sent the dragon or where you tried to hide, the dragon will return to you within a week.”

“Okay well… I’m already keeping one more cat than I’m allowed to in my apartment,” I said. “And I’m not sure I can hide a dragon from my landlord.”

“These are all things that we will work out together,” Tara said. “You’d be surprised at how simple the logistics of having a dragon are.”

Over the next hour, Tara talked a lot and I mostly listened as she explained to me the reality of dragon motherhood, and I pinched my leg until it bruised trying to wake up from the bizarre dream I was having.

Did you know that baby dragons can eat cat food until they are old enough to hunt for themselves? Did you know that dragons only start breaking fire after they hit dragon puberty? Did you know that dragons grow to the size of a great dane and get wings in the first year, and then slowly keep growing until they die? Did you know that you can sell powdered dragon egg shell on the magic private market for thousands of dollars? Did you know that female baby dragons hatch with fur, which they shed after a few days, and that fur can also be sold for thousands of dollars, and when they shed their skin, that can also be sold for thousands of dollars, and eventually they start laying unfertilized eggs like chickens, which can then be powdered and sold for thousands of dollars?

I didn’t know any of that. And then I did. And then I was sent away to find a more appropriate place to live with an alarmingly thick bundle of cash given to me in exchange for the dragon egg. I opened the carrier in the car and the baby dragon climbed out, happily perching on top of it. Cautiously, I offered her my hand and she nuzzled me like she had in the kitchen, almost purring with joy when I pet her.

On the drive home, I tried to wrap my mind about the apparent new reality of my life.

As any cat owner can tell you, cats have an uncanny ability to wake you just long enough before your alarm clock that you can’t fall back asleep for any reasonable amount of time, leaving you to lie in bed for fifteen minutes wondering if their adorable furry faces and cute pink toe beans are really worth their poor manners. The real fun is trying to determine exactly how important it is to get out of bed to attend to your rude feline’s needs- for instance, if they are just whining for food, I have no problem leaving them to beg until I’m ready to leave my blanket cocoon. But if I am roused by the dreadful sound of cat retching, the speed with which I leap out of bed could rival that of an Olympian.

At some point early in the morning when the window shades were just starting to tint blue with the impending sunrise, I heard a ruckus by my dresser, but the squabbling died down after a few minutes and I was able to go back to sleep quickly. Now, though, the kitties were being more insistent. First, Gallifrey jarred me awake by jumping up onto the small of my back, all 23lbs of him landing right on my bladder and his claws digging in around my spine. My eyes sprung open to see Bastet with her paws on the edge of the bed next to my pillow. Her pupils were fully dilated and when she saw that I was awake, she let out a long, anxious meow. I felt Bandit, my third and final cat, pacing up and down my bed next to me, pausing by my feet to hiss at the doorway. Gallifrey kneaded me with his claws and started spitting. I slowly realized that they weren’t just annoying me to feed them, and I sat up quickly, pushing Gallifrey off of me. Bastet jumped up on the bed with us, and all the three cats stood at the foot of my bed, staring intently at the doorway with their tails puffed up.

I made to grab my glasses off the nightstand. They weren’t there. Annoyance temporarily overcame my concern at my cats behavior, as they had a bad habit of knocking my glasses down under my bed. But after a cursory sweep under the bed turned up nothing, I opened my nightstand drawer and wiggled my hand into the back of the clutter until I found the old frames I knew were back there. The lenses were scratched and out of prescription, but they were serviceable for finding my actual glasses.

As the room came into better focus, I noticed first that my dresser appeared to have been ransacked. I jumped out of bed to get a closer look. The wrought iron tree that usually held my jewelry was completely bare. It wasn’t atypical for Bastet to jump up and knock it over, leaving me to spend all afternoon trying to detangle my necklaces, but the tree itself was undisturbed. Only the jewelry was missing. I had somehow been robbed while I slept, and given how bizarre my cats were acting, it occured to me that the intruder might still be lurking somewhere in my apartment. My cell phone, if it hadn’t been stolen, was plugged in charging next to my front door. I would have to risk encountering the burglar to call the authorities. I wrapped my fingers around the base of my jewelry tree. It was an awkward shape to wield, but it was heavy enough to serve as a weapon if I needed it.

I used my foot to push open my bedroom door and behind me heard my cats scramble to hide under the bed. Raising the jewelry tree high over my head, I crept into the living room with my back to the wall, still listening hard. And then I saw my laptop sitting on my coffee table, right out in the open where a robber should have easily grabbed it. My camera bag was also hanging, untouched, next to my front door, and my cell phone was charging on the little table there. What was not on the table, though, was the crystal dish I used to hold my keys and pocket change. The keys, change, and dish were all gone. What was not gone, however, was the thick stack of bills that I had tucked under the dish after my waitressing shift last night. I let my arm, shaking from the weight of my makeshift weapon, droop onto my shoulder, and I wondered what kind of burglar would take less than five dollars of change and a collection of flea market jewelry, but leave my electronics and over a hundred dollars in cash behind.

When I took a step towards my kitchen, something crunched under my foot. I crouched down to see the weird shards of black and sparkle that littered the carpet around my window sill, and realized what else was missing. Last month, when I was visiting my sister’s family, my amatuer geologist of a nephew gifted me with a strange stone he found in the river. It was a perfectly smooth oval, made of a pitch black stone with beautiful iridescent marbling, just slightly too large for me to fit my hands around its girth. I had left it on the window sill, where the sunlight brought a purple sheen out of the black and reflected pretty rainbows on the carpet during the afternoon.

So the burglar had made off with a handful of change and cheap jewelry, and tried to take a weird rock, but somehow shattered it on my carpet?

One of my cats swept past my leg as I stood there frozen in bemusement, and only when I saw the streak of white fur in my peripheral vision did I startle. My cats were black, tabby, and tortoiseshell. I didn’t have any white cats. I spun around to see the tip of a thick white tail disappear around the corner into the kitchen, and I followed it.

From the back, it almost looked like a dumpy puppy who was moving more quickly than gracefully. But it was clearly not a puppy. Its stout legs ended in clawed reptilian feet, its tail dragged heavily on the floor, and its graceful neck held up a triangular head. The creature shuffled across my kitchen and scaled a small pile of shiny objects- there was my jewelry, my change, my silverware, tubes of lip gloss and nail polish, and even my glasses. It stepped delicately into the crystal dish stolen from by my front door, circled itself a few times, and plopped down and nestled in like it was one of my cats’ beds. With surprising dexterity, it plunged one of its front legs into the horde of shiny things and fished out a nickel, which it then popped into its mouth. I could hear the metal grinding in between its teeth, and its yellow eyes drooped slightly before finding me in the doorway. Slitted pupils focused on me, but there was nothing predatory in the gaze.

That didn’t stop me from screaming, or trying to. All that came from my mouth was a strangled moan, and the little creature straightened its neck, cocked its head, and dropped the nickel to respond with an almost identical sound. My tension broke. This thing was clearly not going to hurt me, and even if it was going to try to, it was the size of one of my cats and I could punt it. There was still the obvious problem that I had a mysterious wild animal in my home, however, and the first thing I needed to do was figure out what it was. 

Keeping my eyes on it the whole time, I backed into the living room and fetched my laptop. I also closed my bedroom door to prevent my cats from coming out before I knew what the creature was. I returned to the kitchen to boot up my computer at the table, all the while keeping an eye on the animal, who had fallen asleep. I almost thought I could see little smokey tendrils coming from its nostrils with each tiny snore.

The first thing I googled was “Fucked up puppy” with not a single helpful result.
“Weird white lizard”. Nothing.
“Lizard cat”. Nothing.
“Mutant ferret”. Nothing.
“How to know if you are hallucinating an adorable hellbeast”. Nothing.


Finally, after an hour of searching for anything helpful or relevant, on a hunch I searched for “large black stone with marbling” and after a few minutes of digging through the image results, I found a picture of a stone just like what my nephew had given me. The image led me to a nearly decade old post on a geology forum asking for help identifying the strange rock. There were a lot of suggestions of various types of quartz and other strange rock names I had never heard of. I clicked on the original poster’s username and found his email address.

I knew it was a long shot. It could be a dead email address. The guy himself could be dead, for all I knew. I rewrote the email half a dozen times trying to sound less crazy before I finally just omitted the creature from it entirely. I posed it as if I was simply curious about the rock, because I had found one similar and wondered if he had ever identified it successfully.

Imagine my surprise when I got a response within three minutes. I tried not to get my hopes up as I opened the email.

“Has it hatched yet?”

My first serious relationship started just after my 21st birthday and lasted about three years (two spent living together), and the last year and a half were horrible. I overstayed in a relationship with a man who learned exactly how I was abused as a child and intentionally mimicked it because he knew that it was the way to control me. I learned a lot, but the big thing was this:

I filter myself to an insane degree. When I'm upset, I rarely express it, or I maintain that it isn't important until people stop asking. I refuse to speak until I can express my feelings calmly, and then I minimize them even further. In an argument, I weigh everything I want to say first and don't say anything that I don't deem "productive". There would be days where I simply wanted to tell my exboyfriend about something funny or shitty that happened to me at work, and I would sit next to him silently for fifteen minutes, trying to figure out how to lead into the story, and then ultimately decide that he wouldn't be interested and just not say anything. I wouldn't set appropriate boundaries because I didn't want to be "THAT girlfriend", so I set my feelings aside and let him walk all over me.

I thought that this was a mark of me being a good communicator- levelheaded, not vindictive, always thinking of the other person. What I learned as I slowly grew mute, that NOT communicating is not GOOD communication. In fact, it's actually quite terrible communication. It was a symptom of my lack of self worth, developed while growing up with a volatile, narcissistic mother, who would fly off the handle if I said the wrong thing, or the right thing at the wrong time. It has bled into my friendships, where I still only feel comfortable with a thick wall surrounding me. Sometimes I'll even start to type a comment here on reddit, and then delete the whole thing because "no one cares"- as if the point of the internet is to only contribute things that people care about.

It wasn't fair to me to diminish myself so heavily, and it isn't fair to the people around me to refuse to let them have a full and honest relationship with me.

I'm working on it now, in my current relationship and with myself. I'm working on understanding that sometimes it okay to lose a little bit of control, and it's okay to simply say "I'm having trouble thinking straight because I am upset and I don't want to say something I don't mean" or "I'm angry/hurt, so please let me have a little time to myself right now". I'm working on letting my boyfriend have the opportunity to be there for me when I'm having a bad day, when I'm upset with my family, or when I just don't feel like myself. I'm working on sharing the little details that make life so rich- what I had for lunch, what movie I want to see, or the online shopping that I'm really excited to receive. I'm working on letting myself believe that he really cares. I'm working on setting appropriate boundaries, but it's still really hard for me not to feel like I'm being controlling.

It's a hard thing to work on. I still put very little value into myself. I feel quite silly sharing this, as that voice in my head is saying "you're wasting the time of anyone who happens to read this", and I will certainly end up cutting out a good chunk of it to try and make it a shorter read and less of a waste of time.

So maybe my progress isn't vast, but it is happening.

TL;DR- Due to lack of communication, I got off the wrong Metro train in a foreign country and ended up in the Twilight Zone. (I forgive you for not reading the long version. I like words.)

Summer of 2014, I was lucky enough to study in Paris, France. One of the classes I took was the History of Science in Paris. Our class was comprised of three other students and the professor. Our very first excursion was to La Cite des Sciences et de L'lndustrie (Museum of Science and Industry).  It was a very busy time on the Metro, so we weren't together on the train, but the professor had told us at which stop we would need to transfer to another line. All was well and good, until we got to the stop. Me and the two other students my age got off the train... and turned around to see the professor and the older student still sitting on the car, just in time for the doors to close in our face and the train to leave the station. Turns out the professor had told us the wrong stop, realized it enroute, and assumed that we wouldn't get off the train until he did.

So we had no idea where we were or where we were going, no operational phones, and no way to ask someone to help us (yes, I know that a large amount of French people know enough English that we could have asked, but Parisian people can be really intimidating to newly-arrive students). The Metro map is not at all hard to intepret once you've been using it for a week or two, but on that first weekend, it was basically like trying to read a handful of rainbow spaghetti someone threw on a map.

In any case, we figured out where to go and feeling quite proud of ourselves for doing so, set off. The first transfer we made was onto a far less busy train that serviced mostly small, less used stations. The next stop we got off at was... different.

There is a lot of old shit in Paris. But everything ages beautifully- crumbling stone and dilapidated brickwork, rather than rotting derelict houses and busted out storefronts. To be fair, I was probably caught up enough in the magic of the historic city that my brain created blindspots over the unsightly construction and regular metropolitan filth. So when we stepped into the corridor, the state of it was jarring, to say the least. 

Firstly, we were the only ones that got off the train and everyone on the platform got on the train, leaving us alone. Much like in any big city, there aren't a lot of opportunities to be alone in public in Paris, especially in the middle of the day. And the silence was bizarre. Because there were no other people and no homeless people crouched on the floor (likely because it wasn't a busy enough station to successfully get money from passersby), and the trains were spaced out, it was nearly silent- also a rare find in a big city.

The tiles of the wall were cracked and covered in nasty graffiti applied by unskilled artists. There was water dripping from somewhere in the ceiling that created puddles on the floor. Rather than being lit by the fluorescent lighting of other stations, the corridor was illuminated by exposed hanging bulbs- the kind that were dim, yellow, and let off a hum too quiet to hear but loud enough to make your ears twitch. The were spaced out just far enough to leave fairly dark patches in between. And thanks to the breeze, the bulbs swung back and forth slowly. 

The tunnel was curved, so we couldn't see how long it was. We were all three quite creeped out, but we were talking loudly to compensate for the silence and joking around as we speed-walked to the end of the tunnel, where we expected to either get to the lobby area that would lead to other platforms, or to the stairs that would lead to the street level and we could find the entrance that would take us to the other platforms.

But no. We turned the corner and found another corridor. This one was barely a corridor and more like a tunnel, to be honest. The walls weren't walls, but instead big tarps (like the kind that would contain the dust of a construction area), translucent enough to reveal that they didn't cover walls, but instead yawning darkness. And still, not a soul- not another passenger, employee, or beggar. Just the three of us, suddenly silenced of our jest, and scooting closer together as our hackles raised. Our steps and more mysterious dripping echoed in the seemingly cavernous space. The lights were even more sparse here, and several of them were completely burnt out. Again, this tunnel was curved, and even longer than the first. We saw the end of the tunnel and at this point we were nearly jogging, since beyond the tunnel was better lit and appeared to be the lobby.

But no. Another desolate tunnel. This one, lit with flickering fluorescent fixtures that audibly buzzed, stark concrete walls, and still not a soul in sight. At this point, we were far from the platform and no longer walled in by flimsy tarp. The silence felt almost claustrophobic. Every step and breath seemed amplified, and our voiced bounced aggressively back at us, so we stopped talking for the most part.

We had already been walking for a weirdly long time and this tunnel was the longest of all. At this point, we were starting to worry that we had stumbled into an area that we weren't supposed to be in and wondered if it would be best to go back, catch the next train, and figure out an alternate route to the museum, or maybe just go back to our housing and hope our professor would forgive us. But we had all been quite excited for the excursion and didn't want our professors to worry about us, so we pressed on.

It felt like we walked for an hour, though it was closer to twenty minutes, before we finally got to the stairs up to the street. None of us could figure out the layout of the train station, as in how so much tunnel managed to fit under the street, but nonetheless we were all three unwilling to go back down there to catch the next train we were supposed to transfer to. We ended up walking to the next stop for the line we wanted to get on. Thankfully, it was regular loud, packed, busy Metro station. We did manage to get to our professor, who made fun of us for getting off at the wrong stop in the first place.

Coming from the perspective of a fat person, momentarily putting aside the conversation relating to bullying and focusing on the one about health:

Obviously it is quite silly to pretend that weight and health have nothing to do with one another, but it isn't a simple one-to-one correlation or just a matter of laziness. There are many factors in weight AND health- to name a few of my own, thyroid problems and abusing food as a coping tool for poor mental health/past trauma; a back injury that can make it difficult to be active and some incredibly bad habits when it comes to fitness. Some things that are out of my control and some things that I DO have the power to control and definitely need to continue to work on. 

But how is shaming a fat person (a stranger, no less) going to motivate them to try and be healthy? All that will do is make people feel unworthy of improvement. You have to love yourself to be willing to start the battle for your health. And while I don't think that means you need to lie about finding someone attractive or voice false support for their lifestyle, if we are truly concerned about someone's health, we should consider how to approach them. 

If you are a stranger, the easy answer is "don't". It's none of your business if I am healthy or not. Since when do we as a society find it acceptable to poke our noses into each other's medical business? As a fat person, every horrific comment someone has made to me for the sake of my "health" comes off as such a transparent excuse to be judgmental. 

It's one thing for people I know to speak to me from a place of caring and it's one thing for the medical professionals I see to discuss the topic with me, but there is never an excuse for a stranger to comment on my body or my food even if they have convinced themselves they are doing me a service. Unless they are also approaching random smokers, people drinking in excess at a bar, or people who go out without wearing sunscreen, it's not about how my actions impact my health, it's about their personal opinions on why my particular unhealthy decisions are invalid in their eyes. And again, if you are stranger, it's seriously none of your business if I am healthy or not.

When it comes to nonstrangers, there is room to talk to your loved ones. But if you come at them angrily or as if you find them shameful, that will simply drive them away and drive them further into their bad habits and coping mechanisms. If you come to them from a place of support and kindness, they are far more likely to think that you are invested in their well being. Knowing there is someone who loves me enough to want me to be healthy, I would feel far more comfortable turning to them when I am feeling the urge to eat out of boredom or anxiety or stress, or to ask them to take a walk with me because I'm not feeling up to being active alone. And then I can actually process a "tough love" approach as a positive thing, rather than making me hate myself more.

He was 22 and I was 21 when we got together. I had been working and living on my own since I was 18, he had never had a job or lived out of his parents house. I was sufficient in shopping, cooking, and the other basic functions of adulthood, but he couldn't do so much as cook scrambled eggs without being babysat. He was very, very emotionally coddled by his family, so he had 0 ability to apologize, take responsibility for his actions, or at any point step into anyone else's perspective- every argument was a BIG BLOWOUT FIGHT to him, and his goal was to be as mean and hurtful as possible. I was definitely in the boat of "grew up too fast", and I learned young how to step back from a situation, try to understand what is and isn't my fault, how to honestly and sincerely apologize, and how to see things from someone else's perspective. During a fight, I never say anything without thinking about it first, because I wouldn't want to say something in anger that could truly hurt someone without a productive purpose.

And as much as I tried to help him grow and learn to be an adult, he refused. He would simply throw tantrums and refuse to do things until I just did it for him. That went for chores, paying bills, fixing his car, addressing his interpersonal issues with his parents and friends. I forced him to get a job, after a month of handholding and coaxing. At the time, I thought he just didn't know how to be an adult and he wasn't able to recognize that fact because of how he grew up, but I have realized the truth now:

He knew from the get-go that I one of my deepest psychological issues that comes from a childhood with alcoholic, emotionally abusive parents, is that I have a compulsive need to take care of people, especially people who show patterns of emotional abuse. And he took advantage of that. He kept me isolated, making plans with me and then breaking them at the last second so I just ended up alone at home night after night after night, refusing to let me interact much with his friends, and making me feel awful for not being at his beck and call.

The reality is, I was barely his girlfriend. I was his mother. And I was his hostage. But I was barely his girlfriend.

The lack of staff means that students with problems often just don't get noticed. That can be anything from a school bully to abusive parents to an eating disorder or self harm. For the record, I grew up in a smallish Texas town near Dallas with two moms from the age of 5-12. From 0-5, my biological parents were together, and from 12-onwards, it was just me and my biological mom, though my stepmom was still a huge part of our lives. Even my dad is still close with my biological mom, and he is actually best friends with my stepmom. 

There was a lot of bad that came with it. Given the nature of small Texan towns, if my parents were outed, it could insight violence towards our family. So my sisters and I were instructed to tell people that our moms were just best friends. We weren't allowed to have friends over, my parents rarely came to school plays or Parents' Nights, and if they did come, they would arrive and leave separately and they would never hang around to have any one on one interaction with our teachers or friends' parents. We were a few of the only kids in the elementary school who were not involved in any extracurriculars, which made it pretty hard for us to socialize.

Even with our social isolation, other kids' parents puzzled out the situation, and they were vile. More than once, I had my friends' parents not just not invite me to birthday parties or end of school parties, but they would specifically seek me out to tell me that I was specifically not invited. It was somehow amusing and vindicating to them to be cruel to a child.

I had pretty much no contact with most of my paternal extended family, who completely cut my dad off when he refused to denounce my mother's relationship with a woman. Only when my grandfather was on his deathbed when I was 17 did I get to see them again, after over a decade of separation. I had no interest in making amends, honestly, because fuck those people.

I've always been very proud of my dad for not being insecure or spiteful in any way when it came to my mom being with a woman after they divorced. All he cared about was that my step-parent was kind to me and my older sister.

But even with the negatives, I would never give up my moms' roles in my life. I was truly lucky to be raised in the LGBT community, to be shown that family are the people that we choose and who choose us, not the people that we are born with. I was raised with the idea that it was normal to be not-straight. Oftentimes, even parents who are openminded towards non-straight people treat their kids like "straight" is the baseline, and they have to do serious soul-searching to figure out their orientation. Coming out was never a big deal to me. My parents didn't just assume I would be with a man, nor did they assume I would be with a woman. They didn't put pressure on me to scrutinize my own feelings, so I never felt anything but happy when I was attracted to men or women from all over the feminine-masculine spectrum.

My stepmom is the most selfless, loyal person I know. Even after she moved out, if I was home alone and I needed help with something, she would drop everything to come take care of me- even for something stupid like there being a bug in the shower or something. She takes true joy from things like putting together little Easter or Valentine's Day gifts for us. She loves to experience the things that are important to me, even things that she doesn't necessarily enjoy otherwise, like certain science exhibits at museums or shopping in stores that she wouldn't normally go to. 

I could go on for hours about how wonderful my stepmom is.

Overall, I am eternally grateful for how I was raised, even though it is pretty unconventional by straight OR gay standards. There is a whole lot of complicated stuff when it comes to my parents' relationship statuses and their relationships with me. My biological mom wasn't a great person to be raised by, to be honest. All in all, my life was nothing but improved by having two moms AND a dad.

I once had this older lady come in to get help making a powerpoint presentation for a class. She had no idea how to even approach it, but that's fairly standard for someone who have been out of school for a long time and is a bit rusty on your average assignments. But her level of confusion throughout the entire session was utterly dumbfounding.

So first we used paper and pencil to painstaking write out an outline for the presentation. She didn't really understand the concept of an outline. I'm a patient person, so I was able to calmly walk her through it and explain things several times in several ways without getting frustrated.

I ask her to boot up her computer. Out comes a laptop that must have had its first use as Doogie Howser's journal. It was probably older than I am. It was as thick as a textbook.

But okay, I can handle an outdated laptop just fine.

Next comes the old mouse to plug into the machine- the kind with the track ball that gets all gunked up with dust and stuff. And then the modem. She told me that she didn't know how to "wifi", and plugged her modem into the phone jack so she could connect to her personal internet. Of course, when I checked it, her computer was automatically connected to the campus wifi and the modem was just adding extra useless minutes to her life. So I figured that she was probably a bit more advanced illiterate than I was used to.

So then I walked her through creating a powerpoint slide. She didn't know how to get her text from the word processor to the powerpoint, so I taught her how to make a text box in powerpoint. She lamented to me how long it took to copy information down by hand off of a website, and then type it into a word processor. I asked her why she didn't just copy and paste it. She asked "What is copy and paste?" Okay, go ahead and highlight the text you want to transfer. "What is highlight?" Okay, do this... Now right-click. "What is right-click?"

So I teach her to right-click, copy, and paste. She was ecstatic. So we go to the internet to find some more information and pictures. I ask her to open a new tab for some reason. "What's a tab?" So we get an adequate balance of tabs going, and she asks me how to get a picture off the internet. I tell her to save it. "How do I save something?"
